title: The Network Is More Of Nvidia’s Computer Than It Ever Was At Sun
gist: Nvidia's Q2 FY2027 results show datacenter demand running roughly 30-40% ahead of supply amid CPU, DRAM and HBM shortages across the industry, with purchase commitments more than doubling to $279 billion and networking silicon (InfiniBand, Ethernet, NVSwitch) holding at nearly 20% of datacenter revenue as rackscale GPU systems require double the networking spend of traditional scale-out architectures.

insights.claim: Intel's Q1 2026 disclosure that its CPU supply shortfall was 'a number that started with a B' (billions of dollars) implies the Xeon server CPU shortage was at least 20 percent and probably closer to 25 percent of demand.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: A persistent double-digit CPU supply gap supports pricing power for Intel and AMD server CPUs into 2027-2028 and is a leading indicator for datacenter capex bottlenecks beyond just GPUs.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'Back in April, when Intel reported'

insights.claim: AMD's Epyc over-demand relative to supply may be even higher than Intel's, perhaps 30 percent and growing, as agentic AI drives a renewed surge in CPU capacity needs inside AI datacenters.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Signals AMD's server CPU business has room to keep growing share/pricing even without new product cycles, driven by AI-datacenter host-CPU attach rather than just core-count competition with Intel.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'Back in April, when Intel reported'

insights.claim: Multiple server OEMs have indicated their component demand is running 25 to 30 percent higher than what suppliers can deliver in recent quarters.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Confirms the supply constraint is systemic across the server supply chain, not specific to one vendor, reinforcing a multi-year capacity-buildout investment case across CPU, memory and networking suppliers.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'Back in April, when Intel reported'

insights.claim: Nvidia CFO Collette Kress said the company has enough component supply lined up to grow its datacenter business by slightly more than 70 percent in fiscal 2028.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: A concrete, company-guided growth floor for FY2028 datacenter revenue that investors can use to sanity-check consensus estimates.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'With fiscal 2027 components long since allocated'

insights.claim: Jensen Huang indicated Nvidia is on track to double revenue in fiscal 2027 and suggested it could have doubled again in fiscal 2028 absent shortages in DRAM, HBM, flash and other components, implying unconstrained demand is running nearly 40 percent above current supply.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: If true, Nvidia's revenue ceiling is set by memory (DRAM/HBM) and component supply chains rather than by GPU demand itself, making memory capacity (SK Hynix, Samsung, Micron) the binding constraint to watch for Nvidia's growth trajectory.
insights.quote: The unconstrained would be a lot higher. We will grow 100 percent year over year this year. The unconstrained, you know, is significant, and so we are just going to have to go work hard to get more capacity.
insights.locator: Jensen Huang quote on unconstrained demand

insights.claim: Nvidia's total purchase commitments reached $279 billion by the end of Q2 fiscal 2027, up 2.3 times from $119 billion at the end of Q1 fiscal 2027.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: A more-than-doubling of forward supply commitments in a single quarter is a hard signal of how aggressively Nvidia is locking in capacity (and capital exposure) ahead of demand.
insights.locator: paragraph on purchase commitments of $279 billion

insights.claim: Nvidia's current purchase commitments span the remainder of calendar 2027 through fiscal 2029, with only a small portion allocated to fiscal 2030 and beyond.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: The commitment horizon suggests Nvidia's visibility and supplier contracting currently extend about two to three years out, useful for modeling how far forward the AI capex cycle is actually locked in versus speculative.
insights.locator: paragraph on purchase commitments of $279 billion

insights.claim: The author expects Nvidia's purchase commitments to keep growing to cover roughly $1 trillion in combined Grace-Hopper NVL72 and Vera-Rubin NVL72 system sales already penciled into order books across fiscal 2027 (an estimated $365 billion) and fiscal 2028 (an estimated $625 billion).
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Puts a rough dollar figure on Nvidia's rack-scale NVL72 platform backlog across two fiscal years, a benchmark investors can compare against actual reported bookings each quarter.
insights.locator: paragraph on purchase commitments of $279 billion

insights.claim: If supply constraints ease, or if Nvidia scales back DRAM and HBM memory content per GPU/CPU/DPU unit to sell more total units, its purchase-commitment and revenue figures could move even higher than current projections.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Flags an underappreciated lever: Nvidia could trade memory density per accelerator for higher unit shipments if memory supply stays tight, changing the revenue mix without changing headline unit growth.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'And if supply suddenly becomes less constrained'

themes.theme: Q2 FY2027 financial results and R&D economics

insights.claim: Nvidia's July-quarter (Q2 fiscal 2027) revenue was $96.22 billion, up 105.9 percent year on year, nearly hitting the $100 billion mark in a single quarter.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Confirms revenue is still growing at over 100% year-on-year even at Nvidia's current scale, an unusually durable growth rate for a company of this size.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'In the July quarter'

insights.claim: Operating income rose 124.1 percent year on year to $63.73 billion and net income rose 125.9 percent to $59.96 billion, with net income representing 62 percent of revenue — a margin level public companies rarely attain, though slightly leaner than the record share posted in Q4 fiscal 2026 and Q1 fiscal 2027.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: The margin compression (even if slight) versus prior record quarters is a data point worth tracking for whether component cost inflation or mix shift is starting to erode Nvidia's historically extreme profitability.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'To be precise'

insights.claim: Nvidia spent $7.05 billion on R&D in the quarter, more than double what it spent two years earlier, and the author frames this spending as driving roughly 35 to 40 times that amount in revenue in the quarters that follow.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: A rough R&D-to-revenue multiplier investors can use to judge whether Nvidia's R&D growth rate is under- or over-shooting its own historical return-on-R&D pattern.
insights.quote: It is a nearly perfect money making machine, and very close to a printing press that prints chips and gathers up printed money in exchange.
insights.locator: paragraph on R&D spend of $7.05 billion

insights.claim: The author contrasts Nvidia's R&D reinvestment model with IBM's roughly $200 billion in share buybacks during the 1990s and 2000s, arguing IBM would have been better served investing that capital in building a future business rather than propping up its stock and executive compensation.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: A capital-allocation framework worth applying to today's hyperscalers and chipmakers: sustained aggressive R&D/capex reinvestment (Nvidia-style) versus buyback-heavy capital return (IBM-style) as a long-run predictor of competitive position.
insights.quote: Imagine if International Business Machines believed in its future and instead of spending $200 billion in share buybacks to appease Wall Street and make its top brass rich (sort of) in the 1990s and 2000s, it took that money and invested it in a future it created.
insights.locator: IBM buyback paragraph

insights.claim: Nvidia's Compute & Networking group, covering datacenter and some edge products, generated $88.3 billion in sales in Q2 fiscal 2027, up 113.6 percent year on year.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Datacenter-adjacent compute and networking now represents the overwhelming majority of Nvidia's total business ($88.3B of $96.22B), underscoring how narrow the company's remaining non-datacenter exposure is.
insights.locator: paragraph on Compute & Networking group

insights.claim: Nvidia's Graphics group (PC gaming plus workstation/professional-visualization GPUs) brought in $7.92 billion in the quarter, up 46.4 percent year on year, but the author characterizes it as 'almost noise' relative to the datacenter business.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Confirms gaming/PC GPU exposure is now immaterial to Nvidia's overall investment thesis, which is now almost entirely a datacenter/AI-infrastructure story.
insights.locator: paragraph on Graphics group

insights.claim: Nvidia reclassified its automotive electronics, graphics (gaming/pro-vis), and nascent workstation businesses into a new combined segment called Edge Computing, separate from its core Datacenter division.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: The reclassification itself is a signal of how Nvidia now frames its own business internally — essentially two divisions, Datacenter and everything-else-bundled-as-Edge — useful for adjusting segment models going forward.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'Which is why Nvidia has reclassified'

insights.claim: Nvidia's Datacenter division is now split into Hyperscalers (including large cloud builders) and a combined AI Clouds/Industrial/Enterprise group Nvidia calls ACIE; Hyperscale revenue was $48.71 billion (up 104 percent year on year) versus ACIE revenue of $40.31 billion (up 134.2 percent).
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: ACIE's faster growth rate (134% vs 104%) shows neoclouds, sovereigns and enterprise/industrial AI buyers are now growing faster than the traditional hyperscalers within Nvidia's book, a shift worth tracking for customer-concentration risk.
insights.locator: paragraph on hyperscale portion of datacenter business

insights.claim: The author suspects neoclouds, a handful of sovereign AI buyers, and former HPC-only national labs now doing AI/HPC work together account for the bulk of revenue inside Nvidia's ACIE (AI Clouds, Industrial, Enterprise) segment.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: If correct, neocloud/sovereign AI buildouts are now a large and fast-growing enough customer category to materially move Nvidia's reported numbers, not just a rounding error next to hyperscalers.
insights.locator: paragraph on hyperscale portion of datacenter business

themes.theme: Networking's rising share of the rackscale system

insights.claim: The author's own model estimates Nvidia datacenter compute revenue rose 111.5 percent to $71.57 billion in Q2 fiscal 2027 while datacenter networking revenue rose 140.7 percent to $17.45 billion, with networking growing faster than compute.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Networking outgrowing compute inside Nvidia's own datacenter revenue mix supports the article's central thesis that interconnect, not just accelerator silicon, is now a primary growth driver and revenue pool for Nvidia.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'That brings us to the further drilldown'

insights.claim: Within the author's modeled networking revenue, Quantum-X InfiniBand sales rose 58.9 percent to just under $7.5 billion, with the remaining roughly $10 billion split into an estimated $5.46 billion of Ethernet and $4.5 billion of NVSwitch revenue.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Gives investors a modeled product-level breakdown of Nvidia's networking revenue mix (InfiniBand vs Ethernet vs NVSwitch) that isn't disclosed directly by the company, useful for tracking Spectrum-X Ethernet's share gains against InfiniBand over time.
insights.locator: paragraph on Quantum-X InfiniBand sales

insights.claim: Networking represented 19.7 percent of Nvidia's datacenter sales in Q1 fiscal 2027 and 19.6 percent in Q2 fiscal 2027, a stable roughly one-fifth share, which the author says is about double the networking-spend ratio that traditional cloud and hyperscale buyers have historically preferred.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: A stable ~20% networking share is a benchmark investors can watch quarter to quarter; a rising share would confirm deepening rackscale/NVLink architecture adoption, a falling share would suggest customers reverting to cheaper scale-out designs.
insights.locator: paragraph on networking representing 19.7 percent

insights.claim: In rackscale AI systems with NUMA-style links between GPUs, customers must spend roughly twice as much on networking as in traditional node-based scale-out architectures, because the goal is to fuse dozens of individual GPUs into one giant virtual GPU rather than just connecting independent nodes.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: This is the article's core causal mechanism: rackscale/NVL72-style architecture structurally doubles networking's share of system spend versus classic scale-out, which is a durable tailwind for Nvidia's networking (and NVSwitch/InfiniBand/Ethernet) revenue as long as rackscale designs keep winning share.
insights.quote: This is twice the rate of networking that clouds and hyperscalers like, but in a rackscale system with NUMA links between GPUs or XPUs, you have to spend twice as much on networking because you are not just scaling out individual nodes. You are trying to make a giant virtual GPU out of dozens of real and smaller GPUs.
insights.locator: paragraph on networking representing 19.7 percent

insights.claim: The article's title deliberately echoes Sun Microsystems' famous 1984 slogan 'The Network is the Computer,' coined by Sun's fifth employee John Gage (after founders Scott McNealy, Andy Bechtolsheim, Bill Joy and Vinod Khosla), arguing the phrase applies even more literally to Nvidia's current rackscale architecture than it did to Sun's networked workstations in the pre-commercial-internet era.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Frames Nvidia's NVLink/rackscale strategy as the modern, literal fulfillment of a decades-old computing philosophy, useful shorthand for why Nvidia treats networking as core IP rather than a commodity attach product.
insights.locator: closing paragraph on Sun Microsystems
